newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's Zulu leader says defection was betrayal.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's Zulu leader says defection was betrayal.

text.p: A former political adviser to Inkatha leader Chief Mangosuthu Buthelezi defected to South Africa's ruling African National Congress (ANC) on Thursday in what Buthelezi called "the ultimate betrayal."
"I want to be part of the new South Africa, I want to know what it is like to be free," Walter Felgate, 66, told a news conference in the eastern port city of Durban.

Sporting an ANC baseball cap and waving his new party card, Felgate, who counselled Buthelezi through several rounds of brinkmanship ahead of the country's first all-race elections in 1994, accused his former leader of intolerance.

"It is the ultimate betrayal," Buthelezi told national radio later. "When you have a good relationship like I had with him over so many years, and for him to turn around and do this - it shakes me to my roots and my confidence in human nature."
Buthelezi, fuelling speculation that Felgate quit because his Inkatha career had run out of steam, said he had not been close to his former adviser for the past year.
While the Inkatha Freedom Party lashed out at Felgate the ANC remained silent, though a party source said Felgate was likely to be more of an embarrassment that an asset.

Felgate said disagreement with Buthelezi, President Nelson Mandela's strongest black rival despite being interior minister in the national unity government, and a lack of democracy in Inkatha had led him to quit.

The IFP won control of its stronghold, KwaZulu-Natal province, in the 1994 election, but failed to extend its support nationally and is now losing support in the province and facing financial trouble ahead of the 1999 elections.
Felgate, white bearded and haggard after a year of ill health and major heart surgery, said Inkatha's continual resort to confrontational politics had proved too much for him.
"The lack of democracy inside the IFP, the decisions that are forced on the IFP by the chief (Buthelezi)...make it extremely difficult to work from within the IFP," he said.
Felgate's fiery influence had waned since the 1994 elections, which won him a seat in parliament he later gave up in favour of a seat in KwaZulu-Natal's provincial legislature.
His erstwhile colleagues were stinging in their remarks after his defection to the party he spent most of his recent political life condemning.
